## Solution

We seek $P(2) = \sum_{p\in\mathbb{P}} \frac{1}{p^2}$, the prime zeta function at $s=2$.

### Step 1: Relate $P(s)$ to $\log\zeta(s)$

The Euler product for the Riemann zeta function is
$$\zeta(s) = \prod_{p\in\mathbb{P}} \frac{1}{1-p^{-s}}, \qquad \Re(s)>1.$$

Taking logarithms:
$$\log\zeta(s) = -\sum_{p\in\mathbb{P}} \log(1-p^{-s}) = \sum_{p\in\mathbb{P}} \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{p^{-ks}}{k} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k}\sum_{p\in\mathbb{P}} p^{-ks} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{P(ks)}{k}.$$

### Step 2: Möbius inversion

The relation $\log\zeta(s) = \sum_{k\ge 1} \frac{1}{k}P(ks)$ is a Dirichlet-type convolution. Applying Möbius inversion (with $f(s)=\log\zeta(s)$ and $g(s)=P(s)$, where $f(s)=\sum_{k\ge1}\frac{1}{k}g(ks)$):

$$P(s) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{\mu(k)}{k}\log\zeta(ks),$$

where $\mu$ is the Möbius function. Setting $s=2$:

$$\boxed{P(2) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{\mu(k)}{k}\log\zeta(2k).}$$

### Step 3: Numerical evaluation

Using $\zeta(2n)=\frac{(-1)^{n+1}B_{2n}(2\pi)^{2n}}{2(2n)!}$ (so each $\zeta(2k)$ is a known rational multiple of $\pi^{2k}$), the series converges rapidly since $\zeta(2k)-1\to 0$ exponentially:

| $k$ | $\mu(k)$ | $\frac{\mu(k)}{k}\log\zeta(2k)$ |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $+1$ | $+\log(\pi^2/6) = +0.497700303\ldots$ |
| 2 | $-1$ | $-\tfrac12\log(\pi^4/90) = -0.039556\ldots$ |
| 3 | $-1$ | $-\tfrac13\log(\pi^6/945) = -0.005731\ldots$ |
| 4 | $0$ | $0$ |
| 5 | $-1$ | $-\tfrac15\log\zeta(10) = -0.0001988\ldots$ |
| 6 | $+1$ | $+\tfrac16\log\zeta(12) = +0.0000410\ldots$ |
| 7 | $-1$ | $-\tfrac17\log\zeta(14) = -0.00000875\ldots$ |
| $\ge 10$ | — | $< 10^{-6}$ total |

Accumulating:
$$P(2) = 0.497700303 - 0.039556 - 0.005731 - 0.000199 + 0.000041 - 0.000009 + \cdots$$

$$P(2) = 0.4522474200410654985\ldots$$

### Conclusion

The series has no known closed form in elementary constants; its exact value is given by the Möbius-inversion formula

$$\sum_{p\in\mathbb{P}}\frac{1}{p^2} = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{\mu(k)}{k}\log\zeta(2k) \approx 0.4522474200410654985\ldots$$
